I care about fairness and policy, and I’m learning to build things that put them first.

Hi, I'm Zhihanna! I'm a Stanford sophomore studying math and philosophy, and I researched how AI systems moderate content.

I want to design physical products that are built around fairness from the start. Rules usually arrive after a product is already made. Policy decides who a product has to serve, and design and engineering decide whether it does.

So I want to work in between: making devices that are accessible, honest about what they do, and enjoyable for everyone. To get there, I'm learning product design and exploring mechanical engineering alongside math and philosophy.

  1. Crankshaft: a crank on the shaft pushes a connecting rod and slider, which pops the rabbit up.
  2. Cam and follower: an off-center disc lifts a rod, which sways the flowers.
  3. Cam and shaker: a second cam jiggles a plate under the roots. The rocking funnels are shakers too.
  4. Friction wheels: one wheel turns the other just by touching it.
  5. Hand crank: turning it drives the shaft and everything on it.

A moving gardenscape

Made for
DESIGN11, with teammates
Mechanisms
Cams, shakers, friction wheels, and a crankshaft
Status
Finished

An automaton of a greenhouse. A girl with a moving arm and a watering can tends 3D plants inside plexiglass panels, and roots below the garden show an underground world.

It was my first exposure to design. I loved watching ideas from my head turn into something people could touch. It also taught me that making something physical forces you to be specific, because a design that sounds good in your head still has to actually work！

Studying how LLMs moderate content, and how AI represents people

Type
Research assistantship, Stanford HAI, with Dr. Chien
Timeline
January 2026 to June 2026
Status
Finished

My research moved through four stages:

  • January 2026: a literature review on LLM content moderation, linguistic reclamation, and double standards across platforms.
  • January to March: experiments using LLMs for content moderation.
  • April: applying a recourse framework to grey-area misinformation.
  • April to May: a shift to generative AI, asking what recourse looks like for how systems represent people and cultures, and starting a taxonomy of representation.

From the literature: LLMs can read context like sarcasm and reclaimed language and explain their decisions, but they lack calibrated confidence, are sensitive to prompt wording, and inherit bias from their training data. Work on bias in image generators has focused on who appears in outputs, not on how they are depicted.

AI slop in music: a review of the literature

Type
Literature review, written for Shane Culloty at the McCoy Family Center for Ethics in Society
Covers
Defining slop, generative music tools, streaming platform policies, regulation, and open research gaps
Status
Finished

A review of what researchers, platforms, and lawmakers have said about AI-generated "slop" in music. It separates slop from AI-assisted and fully AI-generated music, compares how streaming platforms respond (outright bans, disclosure labels, or no policy at all), and summarizes proposed laws such as the TRAIN Act and the NO FAKES Act.

Its main conclusions: "slop" resists a single definition, the economics of streaming make the problem structural, and detection is still immature. No music-specific research yet tests whether AI labels change what listeners do.

How bright is a black hole that is eating its companion star?

Type
Course exercise, CIERA REACH program (Northwestern)
Tools
Python, NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib
Status
Finished

A Python model of the light a black hole gives off as it pulls matter from a companion star. It converts mass-transfer rates from COSMIC binary-evolution simulations into luminosity, then checks whether an x-ray telescope could detect the system.

In the system I analyzed, luminosity jumps about four orders of magnitude near 6.75 million years, and the black hole becomes detectable after that.

Code on GitHub

Sorting stars by temperature, brightness, and size

Type
Course exercise, CIERA REACH program (Northwestern)
Tools
Python, NumPy, Matplotlib
Status
Finished

A Hertzsprung-Russell diagram built from a small star dataset. Both axes are logarithmic, color shows temperature, and marker size shows radius estimated from the Stefan-Boltzmann relation. The main sequence and the giant stars stand out as separate groups.
